  1                                       EXECUTIVE SUMMARY


 2          My rebuttal testimony responds to issues raised in intervenor direct testimonies. In

 3   reviewing the testimonies and related additional data provided by the applicants, I have

 4   concluded that:

 5       • Intervenor testimonies supporting Route 894 (the "Proposed Route") on the
 6          basis of performance on habitable structures should be closely scrutinized based
 7          on the evidence and the intent of the rule.
 8          o Not All Habitable Structures Are Equivalent - The Environmental Assessment
 9              ("EX') counts every habitable structure the same way regardless of type or use,
10              but a full-time family home warrants far greater protection under the Public
11              Utility Commission of Texas' ("PUCT" or "Commission") routing criteria than a
12              storage, commercial, or industrial facility.
13          o   Non-Opposition Should Not be Construed as Opposition - The habitable
14              structures whose owners do not oppose the CCN with evidence should not factor
15              into the analysis of impacted habitable structures for routing purposes or else it
16              defeats the purpose of an evidentiary hearing.
17       • The Proposed Route threatens the most sensitive portion of the Lampasas River
18         Watershed.
19         o Independent Scientific Recognition - The Lampasas River is protected by a
20            formal Watershed Protection Plan, confirming its ecological significance and
21              vulnerability to the kinds of disturbance a transmission corridor would cause.
22          o   Location Matters More Than Mileage - Link G13 crosses Mill Creek only a
23              few miles upstream of its confluence with the Lampasas River-one of the most
24              vulnerable locations in the watershed-where herbicide runoff or erosion has
25              minimal distance to travel before reaching the River. Crossing fewer total miles
26              of riparian area while traversing the watershed' s most sensitive point is a worse
27              outcome.
28          o Alternatives Are Better - The alternative routes I recommend take more
29            southerly alignments that avoid the Mill Creek crossing at this sensitive location.
30       • The Proposed Route fails to follow existing property boundaries, roads, and
31         compatible rights-of-way ("ROW"), whereas the recommended alternatives
32          consistently perform better.
33          o   Systemic Problem - Multiple intervenors have documented that the Proposed
34              Route bisects their properties rather than following existing linear features.
35              Bisecting properties without following an existing corridor is often inconsistent
36              with mitigating environmental impacts or impacts on the community and affected
37              landowners.
38          o   Alternatives Are Better - All seven alternative routes I identified in my direct
39              testimony outperform the Proposed Route on the EA' s paralleling metrics.
40

  1                    B.       Not all habitable structures are equivalent.
 2       Q.           DOES THE NUMBER OF HABITABLE STRUCTURES ON A ROUTE

 3                    REFLECT THE ROUTE'S ADVANTAGE ON THIS CRITERION?

 4       A.           Not without important qualifications. The raw count of habitable structures within

 5                    500 feet of route centerline is a relevant starting point, but it is not, and should not

 6                    be treated as, a definitive measure of comparative impact. As stated in the direct

 7                    testimony of former PUCT Chairman Barry Smitherman, a simple counting of

 8                    habitable structures within the applicable notice distance "is not a substitute for an

 9                    examination of moderating the impacts on the community or affected landowners

10                    or prudent avoidance."2 And, as the Commission noted when adopting this rule,

11                    "the determination of the impact of a proposed route upon a landowner...is the

12                    subject matter of the hearing."3

13                             The Commission' s policy of prudent avoidance does not ask simply how

14                    many structures are nearby, it examines the nature and severity of the impacts on

15                    the communities and landowners affected.               For example, a primary family

16                    residence, an industrial facility, a seasonal hunting cabin, and an auto salvage yard

17                    would not be given equal concern.

18

     § 22.52 as Approved at the September 25,2002 Open Meeting (Oct. 8,2002).

  1   Q.   PLEASE DESCRIBE THE TYPES OF QUALITATIVE DIFFERENCES

 2        AMONG        HABITABLE        STRUCTURES          THAT      THE     COMMISSION

 3        SHOULD CONSIDER?

 4   A.   There is a wide spectrum of structures that qualify as "habitable" for purposes of

 5        the EA's analysis. At one end: a full-time primary residence where a family lives

 6        year-round, particularly one who has built their personal, financial, and community

 7        lives around the property. At the other end: a commercial or industrial facility, such

 8        as an auto junkyard or an industrial production and testing site, that contains an

 9        office, break room, or laboratory as an incidental feature of its commercial use.

10                The impacts of a 765-kV transmission line corridor differ fundamentally

11        between these two categories. For a full-time family residence, a 200-foot ROW

12        carrying a line of this scale imposes severe and permanent disruption: towers up to

13        198 feet tall within view of every window facing the corridor; conductor noise

14        audible from the property; ongoing electric and magnetic field ("EMF") exposure;

15        recurring herbicide application in the ROW; periodic maintenance activity; and the

16        permanent transformation of the surrounding landscape from a quiet rural setting

17        to an industrial corridor.

18                For a commercial or industrial structure, most of these concerns either do

19        not arise, arise with far less severity, or are already preexisting. A junkyard or

20        heavy-equipment facility is not a place where residents are trying to sleep, raise

21        families, tend organic gardens, or preserve a pristine natural setting. Its owner has

22        already accepted a level of industrial activity incompatible with residential quiet




                                            8
  1        use and enjoyment. The transmission line' s additional impacts on such a property

 2        are materially different from its impacts on a home.

 3   Q.   HOW DOES THIS QUALITATIVE DISTINCTION RELATE TO THE

 4        COMMISSION'S ROUTING FRAMEWORK?

 5   A.   The Commission' s routing framework in Public Utility Regulatory Act ("PURA")

 6        § 37.056(c)(4) and Commission Rule § 25.101(b)(3)(B) are built around qualitative

 7        judgments, not headcounts.       PURA requires the Commission to consider

 8        "community values, " "historical and aesthetic values," and "environmental

 9        integrity"-criteria that demand an understanding of what is actually at stake for

10        the people and communities affected by a proposed route.        Similarly, Rule §

11        25.101(b)(3)(B) requires routes to moderate the impact on the affected community

12        and landowners. Moderating impact requires having evidence of what kind of

13        impact is being moderated and on whom.

14   Q.   HOW DOES THIS ANALYSIS APPLY TO THE PROPOSED ROUTE'S

15        HABITABLE STRUCTURE COUNT SPECIFICALLY?

16   A.   Several of the habitable structures identified along the alternative routes I

17        recommend in my direct testimony are industrial or commercial facilities, not

18        residences. This is particularly true along Link G9, which is used in all of my

19        recommended alternative routes, where at least three structures identified by Joint

20        Applicants as single-family residences are in fact commercial structures in

21        "Harold' s Auto Parts." Compare this to the habitable structures along Link G13,

22        which do in fact appear to be single-family residences.

  1   Q.   HAVE         OTHER INTERVENORS IN THIS PROCEEDING RAISED

 2        CONCERNS ABOUT THE PROPOSED ROUTE'S IMPACT ON WATER

 3        RESOURCES?

 4   A.   Yes. Concerns about the Proposed Route' s impacts on creeks, rivers, and water

 5        quality have been raised by numerous intervenors. This reflects a broadly shared

 6        recognition among the communities and property owners along the route that the

 7        Proposed Route passes through a landscape whose water resources are sensitive,

10        B.      Independent Scientific Recognition.
11   Q.   IS THERE INDEPENDENT SCIENTIFIC RECOGNITION OF THE

12        ECOLOGICAL          SIGNIFICANCE           OF    THE      LAMPASAS          RIVER

13        WATERSHED?

14   A.   Yes. The Texas A&M University System, through its Texas A&M AgriLife

15        Extension Service, has developed and implemented the Lampasas River Watershed

16        Protection Plan (the "WPP"). The WPP was developed in collaboration with local

17        stakeholders, conservation organizations, and government agencies as part of the

18        Texas Commission on Environmental Quality's ("TCEQ") Nonpoint Source

19        Management Program.         Its development reflects a formal, science-based

20        determination that the Lampasas River watershed is ecologically significant and

21        requires active, coordinated stewardship to protect its water quality and ecological

22        integrity.

23



                                           12
  1   Q.   WHY IS THE EXISTENCE OF THE WATERSHED PROTECTION PLAN

 2        SIGNIFICANT TO THE ROUTING ANALYSIS IN THIS PROCEEDING?

 3   A.   First, it represents an authoritative, science-based determination, independent of

 4        this proceeding and the positions of any party, that the Lampasas River watershed

 5        is a resource of recognized regional importance that is vulnerable to exactly the

 6        kinds of land disturbance associated with a major transmission corridor: vegetation

 7        clearing, soil disruption, herbicide application, and erosion.      The Commission

 8        should give substantial weight to this independent determination.

 9                Second, the WPP is not merely a planning document.        It reflects an active

10        investment of public resources and coordinated effort to protect the watershed. A

11        transmission line corridor crossing key tributaries of the Lampasas River at

12        sensitive locations would directly undermine those investments.

13        C.     Location matters more than mileage.
14   Q.   HOW DOES THE LOCATION OF THE PROPOSED ROUTE'S RIPARIAN

15        CROSSINGS COMPARE TO THOSE OF THE ALTERNATIVE ROUTES?

16   A.   The critical distinction is Mill Creek. As described in my direct testimony and in

17        the testimony of Mr. Sneed, Link G13 crosses Mill Creek at a location that is only

18        a few miles upstream of Mill Creek's conf[uence with the Lampasas River. This is

19        among the most sensitive locations in the watershed for a transmission corridor

20        crossing.

21               The proximity to the Lampasas River is the decisive factor. The closer a

22        contamination source is to the receiving water body, the shorter the distance that

23        contaminants must travel through soil or water before reaching the river, and the

24        less opportunity there is for natural filtration to attenuate those contaminants before

                                            13
  1        they reach the river. A transmission line ROW that crosses Mill Creek within a few

 2        miles of the Lampasas River places a recurring herbicide application program at a

 3        location where its impacts on the Lampasas River are most direct and least buffered.

 4   Q.   ARE THERE ALTERNATIVES TO THE PROPSED ROUTE THAT

 5        PERFORM BETTER ON RIPARIAN CROSSINGS?

 6   A.   The alternative routes I recommend take more southerly alignments that do not

 7        cross Mill Creek at this sensitive location. Even where those routes cross more

 8        total miles of riparian area, those crossings are at locations where the distance to

 9        the Lampasas River or other sensitive water bodies is greater. Crossing slightly

10        more miles of less sensitive riparian area is a better outcome for the watershed than

11        crossing fewer miles while traversing the most vulnerable location in the system.

12   Q.   HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO THE TESTIMONIES OF INTERVENORS

13        ASSERTING THAT THE SAN SABA RIVER NEEDS PROTECTION?

14   A.   While I do not dispute their claims, I would note that the proposed route impacts a

15        greater distance of the Lampsas River and several of its tributaries. In my Rebuttal

16        Attachment A, I provide a map of the Joint Applicant' s proposed route along with

17        my recommended alternative routes and the Lampasas and San Saba Rivers. As

18        may be seen on the map, my alternative proposed routes provide a greater buffer

19        between the transmission line, the Lampasas River water shed, and the Lampasas

20        River itself than the Joint Applicant' s Proposed Route, which is commensurate with

21        the buffer provided for the San Saba River on the Western portion of the proposed

22        transmission line.

 2        Q.      PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY AND YOUR

 3                RECOMMENDATIONS.

 4   A.        My rebuttal testimony may be summarized as follows:
 5                    •   Habitable Structures: Reliance on raw counts of structures within 500 feet

 6                        of route centerline overstates the Proposed Route' s apparent advantage.

 7                        Not all habitable structures are equivalent: a full-time primary residence

 8                        warrants fundamentally greater protection than a commercial or industrial

 9                        structure that happens to satisfy the technical definition of habitability.

10                        Additionally, the habitable structures whose owners do not oppose the CCN

11                        with evidence should not factor into the analysis of the impacts to habitable

12                        structures for routing purposes.

13                    •   Water Resources: The Lampasas River watershed has been formally

14                        recognized as ecologically significant and in need of active protection. The

15                        Proposed Route crosses Mill Creek a few miles upstream of its confluence

16                        with the Lampasas River, making the crossing more impactful than

17                        crossings elsewhere.     The alternative routes I recommend take more

18                        southerly alignments that better avoid this sensitive location.

19                    •   Paralleling Property Boundaries, Roads, and Compatible ROW: The

20                        Proposed Route' s failure to follow existing property boundaries, roads, and

21                        compatible rights-of-way is a systemic problem documented by numerous

22                        intervenors on the Proposed Route.          All seven alternative routes I

23                        recommend outperform the Proposed Route on the EA' s own paralleling

  1               data. On a line of more than 220 miles, the three-to-four percentage point

 2               improvement in paralleling performance translates into many miles of

 3               additional route that follow existing features rather than bisecting

 4               undisturbed rural land.    The Commission' s rules treat paralleling as a

 5                substantive routing obligation, which the Proposed Route does not satisfy

 6               to the extent that the available alternatives demonstrate is reasonable.

 7               I respectfully urge the Commission to reject the Proposed Route or any
